articles.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
articles.summary: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.

blocks.text: "It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.
Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.
The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.

Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.

"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."
With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.
"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."
Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.
Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.
In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.
Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.

This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño.
Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.
But the workers have a huge task on their hands.
Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.
The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.
Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.
Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades

"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.
He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely.
But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.

The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary.
However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers.

"Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."
Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.
Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.
But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.
A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".
So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.
In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.

Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall.

"For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean.
"We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."

The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.
Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.

In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.

The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.
The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.
Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.

It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

articles.title: ‘No one is in charge’: social care system in England in chaos, Louise Casey to say
articles.summary:
Head of major review into adult social care will say that governments have been ‘asleep at the wheel’ of vital system

Successive governments in England have been “asleep at the wheel” on…

blocks.text: Successive governments in England have been “asleep at the wheel” on social care, leaving the system to grow as a chaotic patchwork of local services with no clear vision, Louise Casey, the head of the social care commission, is to warn.

Lady Casey, who is preparing proposals for a big review of adult social care, will say the result is that in effect “no one is in charge” of a system that provides vital services for millions of vulnerable people.

People’s experiences of care have varied depending on where they live, with different standards, assessment processes and waiting times, while the private care sector has grown dominant and regulation of services has often been ineffectual, she will say.

She will add that England has no clear “system stewardship” for social care, making it difficult for governments to target improvements to services or translate policy into practice, unlike in comparable countries such as France, Germany and Japan.

Casey is expected to call for a “new settlement” for care, “one based on values I still believe this country shares: decency, contribution and a duty to care for our neighbours, our loved ones and ourselves”.

Casey’s latest robust critique of adult social care, together with her view that the system faces a “moment of reckoning”, has additional force given Andy Burnham’s ambitions to introduce a new national care service and reform care funding and the workforce.

The prime minister has embraced the Casey review, accelerating its completion to next year – 12 months quicker than envisaged by the Starmer government – with the expectation that a national care service plan will be in Labour’s next election manifesto.

He has already announced he would use savings from scrapping the state pension triple lock, starting in the next parliament, to target investment into a care service based on the Scottish approach of free personal care, with individuals paying for “bed and board” costs.
Speaking at the annual national children and adult services conference on Wednesday, Casey will also say she has written to the Covid-19 inquiry agreeing with its findings on social care.

She is expected to say: “The Covid-19 inquiry took apart the argument that a ‘protective ring’ had been thrown around care homes during the pandemic. Many old people died without their loved ones by their side. Many care workers left their jobs after what they had seen.
“It is a national shame that this was allowed to happen. It should never happen again.”

The Covid-19 inquiry chair, Heather Hallett, last month described the adult care sector during the pandemic as “something of an afterthought”, with care home residents and staff given insufficient protection. More than 43,000 people died from Covid-19 in UK care homes between March 2020 and July 2022.

Casey has drawn on research that highlights how the lack of oversight and a “clear coherent narrative” in English social care is a “significant weakness” in the system, exacerbated by the historic low visibility of social care among successive governments.

The research, by the Nuffield Trust and the Institute for Government, found the lack of clarity in the system made it difficult and slow for policy change to happen. But it warned politicians against embarking on disruptive structural changes without a clear purpose or political determination.
“One last and inescapable point is that successful reform of social care requires political will and bravery to make the choices outlined throughout this report,” it said.

“No amount of reorganisation of governance structures or processes will be sufficient in the absence of political impetus to drive through change and dedicate resources, time and energy to social care. Maintaining social care visibility and priority within the government’s agenda will be essential.”

articles.title: Disabled people in England ‘have to wait up to two years for wheelchairs’
articles.summary:
Ombudsman’s report says delays have profound consequences and limit users’ ability to lead independent lives

Disabled people are having to wait up to two years to get a wheelchair because of…

blocks.text: Disabled people are having to wait up to two years to get a wheelchair because of delays involving NHS bodies and private firms that make them.

The situation is revealed in a report by the parliamentary and health service ombudsman for England, Paula Sussex, who said hold-ups were having profound consequences and limiting wheelchair users’ ability to lead independent lives.

In one case a three-year-old boy with cerebral palsy was unable to start nursery at the same time as his twin brother because he had to wait seven months for a wheelchair. He hurt himself several times when he fell from an adapted buggy his parents were using while they waited.
Sussex launched an investigation into NHS wheelchair provision after a sharp rise in complaints – from eight in 2020-21 to 110 in 2025-26.
Four out of five relate to the handful of private firms that provide wheelchairs to at least half of all children and adults who need one to help them lead independent lives.
Most are about people who need a wheelchair having to wait longer than the supposed 18-week maximum to receive either the device or parts for it.
“For people who rely on a wheelchair, delays, unsuitable equipment or poor repairs can affect every part of their life”, said Sussex.
“There can be profound consequences, from physical pain and emotional distress to limiting their ability to lead full lives.”
Elliot Cruz Gardiyanoglu, now six, was three when he faced a seven-month wait for his wheelchair. That also meant that he was unable access education or specialist therapy.

“We were never told there would be such a long wait for the wheelchair,” his mother, Jania Cruz, said. “If we had known we would have explored other ways to get it, especially so that Elliot did not miss out on starting nursery at the same time as his brother.
“It was very hard for him to see his brother going to school while he couldn’t.”

Rachel Perrin, the director of Newlife, a charity for disabled children, said Elliot’s experience showed how “the wrong wheelchair – or no wheelchair at all – can be dangerous, as well as keeping children and their families trapped at home and leaving them unable to attend school and take part in activities with siblings and friends”.
Graham Woolner, a 68-year-old in Bishop’s Stortford who has spinal muscular atrophy, a degenerative condition, has needed a wheelchair for the last 15 years.

He was meant to get a new one by August 2023 but it did not arrive until September 2024, and when it did, it failed to work properly. He did not get one in full working order until October 2025, 26 months past the 18-week deadline.
after newsletter promotion

“After a year of waiting, the wheelchair they gave me broke on the first day. I only made it 100 yards before the batteries died,” Woolner said. “The battery issue was never resolved, so I couldn’t go anywhere for a year with any certainty that I would get there and back.
“I like to be independent, go into town and take my dogs for a walk. But it got to the point where I wouldn’t go out without my son in case I needed him to push me home.
“The wheelchair is effectively my legs. I need it to live my daily life.”
Nick Goldup, the chief executive of the Wheelchair Alliance, said the report shone a light on the systemic problems wheelchair users faced.
“Getting wheelchair provision right means giving people the freedom to live their lives and to enable them to contribute meaningfully to society,” he said.

Sussex highlights a “regulatory gap” in wheelchair services such as assessment, fitting and repair. The Medicines and Healthcare products Regulatory Agency oversees the equipment, but the remit of the Care Quality Commission – the NHS care watchdog – does not cover the services wheelchair users receive because they are not supervised by a health professional.

Integrated care boards (ICBs), NHS regional bodies that commission wheelchair services, have “unreliable information” about how many people locally need a wheelchair and are faced with “an uncompetitive wheelchair market” which is dominated by a handful of private providers. Nor are ICBs good at telling each other when they encounter problems with private firms that provide poor services.
An NHS spokesperson said:“Long waits for wheelchairs are unacceptable, denying people the independence and quality of life they deserve.

“That’s why our wheelchair quality framework, co-produced with wheelchair users, sets a clear expectation that 92% of people receive their equipment within 18 weeks, and requires commissioners to hold regular performance meetings with providers to identify and tackle delays.”

articles.title: Lapid to Davao City accountant at Duterte trial: 'Are you being used?'
articles.summary: "Nagamit ba kayo?"

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 7:45am

MANILA, Philippines — Expressing frustration over a resource person's repeated inability to answer questions, Sen. Lito Lapid told Davao City Accountant Vingelin Bajan that her apparent lack of knowledge made it seem as though she was merely being used by others.

Lapid's interjection on Tuesday, November 10, came after several rounds of questioning in which Bajan repeatedly said she could not recall key details about her past partnership in an accounting firm that audited several companies linked to Vice President Sara Duterte.
"'Yung mga nakikinig na kababayan natin dito, 'pag hindi kayo nakakasagot, naiinis sila. Kami rin," Lapid said.
(The people listening to this, our fellow citizens, get annoyed when you cannot answer. We do too.)
"Ang iniisip namin, pumunta ka rito, nagagamit ka lang dahil kayo ang city accountant ng Davao na parang wala kayong alam. Sana magsalita kayo ng totoo," he added.
(We are thinking that you came here only to be used because you are the Davao City accountant, yet it seems you know nothing. I hope you tell the truth.)
Bajan, however, insisted that she was not being used.
Earlier, Bajan also drew the ire of senator-judges after repeatedly saying she could not recall details of several transactions and information about her former accounting firm.
She acknowledged that she had been a partner in the accounting firm since its registration in 2003, when she was also working for the Davao City government under a job-order arrangement.

articles.title: LIVE: Sara Duterte impeachment trial, Nov. 11
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte resumes Wednesday, November 11, with the defense set to present another witness in connection with allegations of unexplained wealth under Article…

blocks.text: November 11, 2026 | 7:25am

MANILA, Philippines — The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte resumes Wednesday, November 11, with the defense set to present another witness in connection with allegations of unexplained wealth under Article II of the impeachment complaint.

Lawyer Suzette Balucanag-Punay, corporate counsel for Gencorp Industries Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corp., is expected to testify on corporate and business matters involving the two companies linked to Duterte.
She is also expected to submit certified true copies or original copies of the companies' General Information Sheets, audited financial statements and other corporate records covering 2022 to 2025.
Balucanag-Punay was supposed to testify on Monday but was unable to attend the hearing due to a scheduled MRI scan.

Meanwhile, the defense has dropped Matina Crossing, Davao City barangay chairperson Cindy Colina from its list of witnesses. Colina was initially scheduled to testify on matters concerning the barangay's creation, official name and other names by which it is known.
Watch the proceedings live at 10 a.m. as the Senate impeachment court resumes hearing the defense's case.

articles.title: Slain cartel boss 'The General' provided Ryan Wedding with fake police ID to evade capture, U.S. alleges
articles.summary: U.S. federal charges announced on Tuesday provide new insight into two alleged accomplices accused of helping to protect Canadian Ryan Wedding while he was a fugitive in Mexico.

image.caption: Edgar Aaron Vazquez Alvarado, known as 'The General,' left, is accused of helping alleged drug smuggler Ryan Wedding, right, evade capture in Mexico. Vazquez was shot dead in an operation involving Mexican security forces, Mexico's security minister announced last week. (U.S. Treasury Department/FBI

blocks.text: World
U.S. federal charges announced on Tuesday provide new insight into two alleged accomplices accused of helping to protect Canadian Ryan Wedding while he was a fugitive in Mexico.
New charges give insight into how Canadian drug smuggler avoided arrest in Mexico for a decade
How did Ryan Wedding — the Canadian Olympic snowboarder turned international fugitive — manage to evade capture for a decade in Mexico?

U.S. federal charges announced in California on Tuesday gave part of the answer, providing new insight into two alleged accomplices accused of helping to protect Wedding by using tactics worthy of the Netflix series Narcos.

According to a grand jury indictment unsealed in Los Angeles, cartel leader Edgar Aaron Vazquez Alvarado gave Wedding and other co-conspirators a code word so cocaine loads would not be blocked by Mexican police and military personnel.
The code word changed almost daily.

What's more, Vazquez is accused of providing Wedding and co-conspirators with "authentic law enforcement credentials" that were manipulated to bear their own names, allowing Wedding and others to safely pass through security checkpoints in Mexico.

items: Ryan Wedding murder trial delayed to 2027 due to 'unusual and complex' case

blocks.text: But all that help came at a cost.
$500,000 US entry fee

U.S. prosecutors said Vazquez welcomed the Thunder Bay, Ont.-born Wedding into a club of organized crime leaders who received sensitive information, including details about arrest warrants and investigations.
The indictment, released Tuesday, said Vazquez charged Wedding a one-time initiation fee of $500,000 US to be allowed into the group, and an average monthly fee of $100,000 US.
Mexico Security Minister Omar García Harfuch announced last week that 42-year-old Vazquez — known as "The General" — had been fatally shot in an operation involving Mexican security forces.
Mexican judge accused of taking $2M bribe to free Ryan Wedding's right-hand man

His name was first publicly linked to Wedding a year ago when the U.S. Treasury Department announced sanctions against Vazquez and his companies for their ties to the Canadian. The department identified Vazquez as a former Mexican law enforcement officer with high-level connections.
Wedding, 45, allegedly ran a murderous drug-smuggling network that generated $1 billion US a year. The FBI said he fled to Mexico around the time he faced criminal charges in Montreal in 2015.

items: Ryan Wedding's accused Canadian money launderer agrees to U.S. extradition

blocks.text: Also known as Public Enemy, Wedding was arrested in Mexico in January and remains in U.S. custody. He has pleaded not guilty to a list of charges related to murder and drug trafficking. He is scheduled to stand trial in Los Angeles next year.
Suspect allegedly had ties to notorious cartels
Also in Tuesday's news release, the U.S. Attorney's Office in L.A. identified "reputed street gang member" Roberto Gomez as another key facilitator in Wedding's ability to spend years on the run.
Gomez, who went by the aliases Fat Boy and Rooster, allegedly cultivated relationships with people who had access to sensitive information from Mexican and U.S. law enforcement.

The prosecutor's office said the 51-year-old former L.A. resident also kept in touch with leaders of the Sinaloa and Jalisco New Generation cartels — two of Mexico's most notorious criminal syndicates, considered terrorist organizations by the U.S. and Canada.
Ryan Wedding is escorted off a plane in Ontario, Calif., in January, hours after his arrest in Mexico. (FBI)

While Wedding was on the run, the FBI said he benefited from the protection of the Sinaloa Cartel, which was co-founded by infamous drug lord Joaquín (El Chapo) Guzmán. Further details of Wedding's purported arrangements in Mexico are only now beginning to trickle out.
"There were multiple attempts to capture Mr. Wedding, and in each of those attempts we were undermined," First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli told CBC News last week.
"He either was tipped off or was given a warning, and was somehow always able to evade us, just barely … and so it was our belief that he was getting help."
U.S. authorities allege Gomez provided Wedding with sensitive information to evade capture, and also helped supply him with bulk drug shipments.
In one instance, prosecutors said Gomez attempted to broker the sale of 453.6 kilograms of methamphetamine to Wedding for $550,000 US in cryptocurrency.

items: Ryan Wedding ally 'Tupac,' who allegedly offered cosmetic surgery to locate murder target, requests bail

blocks.text: Gomez, who is listed as a fugitive living in Mexico, faces six charges, including drug offences and one count of attempting to transact and deal with a "specially designated narcotics trafficker."
The charges unsealed against Vazquez and Gomez add to a flurry of law enforcement activity over the past week in the Wedding case.
Ryan Wedding's alleged second-in-command, Canadian Andrew Clark, was arrested in Mexico in October 2024 in an operation involving Interpol and the Mexican navy. (Omar García Harfuch/Facebook)
The FBI announced the arrest in Colombia last week of a Mexican judge accused of accepting $2 million US in bribes to free Wedding's alleged second-in-command, Andrew Clark.

On Wednesday, Mexican authorities are expected to auction off 61 rare and high-performance motorcycles seized last year from properties linked to Wedding. The FBI previously estimated the collection was worth $40 million US.
The U.S. treasury also announced sanctions against Iran-linked firms in the Toronto and Vancouver areas accused of helping Wedding launder billions of dollars in drug proceeds.
CBC News senior reporter Thomas Daigle has extensively covered the case of Ryan Wedding. He can be reached by email at thomas.daigle@cbc.ca.

articles.title: US charges 3 alleged Iranian operatives over plots targeting Jewish communities and a UK airbase
articles.summary: US prosecutors claim the three men were planning a "campaign of terror" ish communities and a UK airbase. The Fairford incident prompted the withdrawal of US bombers stationed there for operations…

image.caption: US bombers stationed at Fairford were withdrawn following the discovery of an alleged plot targeting the baseImage: Alastair Grant/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: US authorities charged three men on Tuesday over allegedly plotting a "campaign of terror," claiming that the trio had planned nearly 20 attacks against Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, as well as Britain's Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford airbase.

The British base was used by the US for attacks against Iran. It came under the spotlight in late September, when UK authorities detained several men over a "major incident" near the military compound.

The officials had received information about suspicious vehicles nearing the base and responded by setting up a safety zone and evacuating homes in the area, as well as by dispatching strong security forces and a bomb disposal unit. Five people were arrested.
The US has since withdrew its bombers from the base.
One of the defendants charged on Friday allegedly helped coordinate the Fairford incident from a US jail.
What do US prosecutors allege?
An updated indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court charged an Iranian-Iraqi dual national, an Iranian national and an Iraqi national. Only the dual national is in custody.
"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran," US Attorney Jamie McDonald said.

Prosecutors claim the dual national used coded messages to relatives from jail to arrange payments to people who could carry out attacks. He allegedly continued coordinating with his co-defendants in the days before the Fairford incident.

The indictment said the men used a network of contacts in Britain to plan attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned network that included Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and the Iraqi armed group Kata'ib Hizballah. Both are designated foreign terrorist organizations by the US.
Suspect says he is a 'prisoner of war'
Prosecutors described the defendant held in the US as a Kata'ib Hizballah commander.
Arrested in the spring, the suspect pleaded not guilty in June to charges of plotting at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the US and Israeli war with Iran.
He called himself a "prisoner of war."
British authorities had also linked the alleged Fairford plot to Tehran, which denied involvement. .
All the Ayatollah's men — ensuring the regime's survival

UK prosecutors alsoseparately charged two men, both 24, under the National Security Act in October. One is accused of assisting Iran's intelligence service and was granted conditional bail. The other faces a charge of entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, relating to an alleged reconnaissance visit to Fairford in August. He was remanded in custody.

articles.title: Canada should not end its Arctic drilling ban, warns former environment minister
articles.summary: As the federal government opens the door to lifting Canada's moratorium on Arctic oil-and-gas drilling, a former environment minister says it's not worth the risk.

image.caption: Former environment minister Steven Guilbeault says opening up Canada's Arctic for oil-and-gas exploration would be dangerous and internationally controversial. (Spencer ColbyThe Canadian Press)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New
As the federal government opens the door to lifting Canada's moratorium on Arctic oil-and-gas drilling, a former environment minister says it's not worth the risk.
Mark Carney says he's consulting with northern communities about whether to keep the moratorium
LISTEN | Interview with former environment minister Steven Guilbeault:
As It Happens6:28Canada should not end its Arctic drilling ban, warns former environment minister
Prime Minister Mark Carney has confirmed news reports that he's consulting with northern governments and Indigenous communities about whether to keep the ban in place.

Finance Department spokesperson Marie-France Faucher told the Toronto Star that $11 million earmarked in the federal budget for Arctic offshore oil-and-gas governance is, in part, for "consideration of potentially lifting the current moratorium."
But at this point, Carney says, it's "absolutely not in any way, shape or form a decision about lifting the moratorium. It is a respectful engagement."
Steven Guilbeault, who served as Canada's environment minister between 2021 and 2025, says Arctic drilling is a bad idea. Here is part of his conversation with As It Happens host Nil Köksal.
Mark Carney says this is all just about consultation with northern communities to find out what they think about potentially lifting this moratorium, this drilling ban. What's wrong with that?

If that's all that it is, then I'm a very happy person. Unfortunately, in the Toronto Star article … there is a finance official who says, on record, that it is potentially to open up oil-and-gas exploration and exploitation in the Arctic.
Budget's offshore gas funding 'absolutely not' a decision to lift Arctic drilling moratorium, Carney says
For you, what are the biggest risks to opening up the western Arctic to oil and gas, potentially?
We hardly have acceptable technologies to clean up oil spills in normal water conditions…. We have no technologies to clean up oil spills where sea ice is involved. There are none.

There are a lot of oil spills happening all around the world at just about any given day of the week … so the question is not: Will there be an oil spill in the Arctic if we start doing that? The question is: When and how much?
And it's a very fragile ecosystem, an ecosystem that we're still learning so much about. And there's so many things we don't understand yet about the fragility of the Arctic ecosystem.

Then there's the issue of whether or not, five years, 10 years down the road — because, really, this is what we're talking about in terms of timeline, if something like that would happen — will there still be a growing demand for oil around the world?

In 2025, one in four vehicles sold in the world was an electric vehicle. By the end of this year, 2026, they will likely be one in three vehicles now that just about everywhere in the world, solar and wind are cheaper to produce electricity than coal or even natural gas.

So I think it begs the question: Why would we do that? Why risk compromising the ecosystem of one of the most pristine places on Earth for something that, if there is an economic case for it, might be very short-lived?

items: 56 top Canadian scientists push for changes to Carney's new major projects bill
Canada can 'definitely' transition to renewables by 2050, expert tells youth climate trial

blocks.text: When you say you're hopeful that what Prime Minister Carney is saying, that this is about discussion at this stage and just discussion, that you would be pleased with that, I mean, are you suggesting that you're not sure that he's representing his plans accurately?
I'm saying we have two contradictory statements here.

We have, obviously, the prime minister saying this is just for consultation. And we have someone from the finance department on record saying, well, actually, no, the goal of what we're doing is to exploit oil and gas in the Arctic.

I'm hoping that, in the meantime, the prime minister and the government came to realize that this will be hugely controversial. It's going to be hugely controversial in Canada. It's going to be controversial in the North. It's going to be controversial internationally.
I am heading to the UN conference on climate change in Turkey. I've been talking to people from all around the world who just can't believe that Canada would even think about doing that.

The Arctic is partly Canadian for sure, but it's an international territory. It's a very powerful international symbol in terms of environmental safeguards and conservation. And I think that the international public outcry would be something we haven't seen very often in Canada.
Interview produced by Chris Harbord. Q&A edited for length and clarity

articles.title: 3 charged in U.S. with planning terror attacks, including alleged planned assault on British airbase
articles.summary: U.S. authorities accused three men Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British…

image.caption: A B1 bomber prepares to take off as police officers guard a checkpoint near RAF Fairford air base in Fairford, England, on Sept. 29. (Alastair Grant/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·New

U.S. authorities accused three men Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S., as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.
1 suspect allegedly continued to co-ordinate U.K. attack after arrest months earlier, U.S. attorney says

Three men, including one already jailed in the United States, were accused by U.S. authorities Tuesday of being Iran-supported operatives who plotted nearly 20 attacks on Jewish communities in Europe and the U.S. as well as a planned assault on a British airbase used by the U.S. Air Force.

Charges against Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, were outlined in a superseding indictment unsealed in Manhattan federal court. Only al-Saadi is in custody.

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald in New York said in a news release that al-Saadi, who was arrested in the spring, allegedly continued to co-ordinate with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted September terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where U.S. bombers and troops had been stationed.

"These defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members," McDonald said. "The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real."
U.K. police arrest 5 near airbase on suspicion of terrorist plot
Attorney General Todd Blanche said: "Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government."

The new indictment offers fresh insight into an episode that has been shrouded in mystery for more than a month after five men were detained after midnight on Sept. 27 on suspected explosives and terrorism offenses after three suspicious vans were spotted travelling toward the base in western England.
A sixth suspect, a British-Iranian dual national, was arrested several days later. All the men were released on bail.

items: U.K. charges 2 men, accuses them of working on Iran's behalf in incident at airbase
Canada, U.K. allies vow action after RAF Fairford terror plot

blocks.text: British authorities linked the incident to Tehran, and though Iran denied involvement, the arrests prompted the U.S. to withdraw its bombers that had been stationed there. The bombers were redeployed to their home bases in the United States.
RAF Fairford, located 160 kilometres west of London, has been used by American bombers during decades of conflicts in the Middle East.
According to the indictment, al-Saadi allegedly used coded language in communications with relatives from jail to direct that money be passed along to others who could carry out attacks.

items: U.S. soldier arrested in England on suspicion of espionage related to Russia, counterterror police say

blocks.text: The indictment alleged that the three men conspired together to use a network of contacts in the United Kingdom to commit terrorist attacks on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) and Kata’ib Hezbollah.

In June, al-Saadi pleaded not guilty to charges that he plotted at least 18 attacks in Europe in retaliation for the U.S. and Israel’s war with Iran. He called himself a "prisoner of war." He has been held without bail since. His lawyers did not immediately respond to requests for comment Tuesday on the latest development.
Both Kata’ib Hezbollah and Iran’s IRGC have been designated by the U.S. government as foreign terrorist organizations. U.S. prosecutors say Al-Saadi was a Kata’ib Hezbollah commander.

articles.title: Tensions between PM, Quebec premier continue to flare in new tiff over U.S. relations
articles.summary: Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon sent letters to U.S. elected officials, as part of his intention to negotiate directly with American states. The move appeared to irritate Prime Minister Mark Carney,…

image.caption: Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke in Montreal on Tuesday, alongside Culture Minister Marc Miller, left, and Industry Minister Melanie Joly, right. During the news conference, he was asked about the Quebec government's intention to negotiate directly with American states. (Graham Hughes/The Canadian P

blocks.text: Montreal·New

Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon sent letters to U.S. elected officials, as part of his intention to negotiate directly with American states. The move appeared to irritate Prime Minister Mark Carney, who said, "in a negotiation, it's always a good idea to have a single negotiator."
Carney rebukes St-Pierre Plamondon's aim to negotiate directly with American counterparts
The relationship between Prime Minister Mark Carney and Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon has gotten off to a rocky start over the past couple of weeks.

The most recent incident happened on Tuesday. Carney was at a news conference in Montreal — highlighting his government's commitment in last week's federal budget to invest in culture — when he was asked about the Quebec government's intention to negotiate directly with American states.

The question came following news that Paul St. Pierre Plamondon had sent letters to 59 newly elected U.S. officials, including Michigan senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed and re-elected governor Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire.

In the letters, the premier wrote about Quebec's trade relationship with each state, and invited the state representatives to work directly with a Quebec delegate on "new projects and initiatives for the benefit of our respective populations."

That gestured appeared to irk the prime minister. When he was asked about the Quebec premier's efforts, Carney pointed out that "the executive branch, the president, and the American courts," are still the decision-makers for agreements and trade initiatives.
"Secondly," he said, "in a negotiation, it's always a good idea to have a single negotiator."
He then stated that this responsibility lies with the federal government.
'Mr. Carney is not my boss,' says Quebec premier
St-Pierre Plamondon responded to Carney's comments by doubling down.
“Mr. Carney dreams of us not putting on our skates and never setting foot on the ice because he wants the rink all to himself," he said.
"Welcome to Quebec. We have always asserted our place."

items: Before a referendum, how a new PQ government could test Ottawa

blocks.text: He said the letters are something other governments have done before, and that he's doing what he believes is in the best interest of the province.
"And Mr. Carney is not my boss, and he will not prevent Quebec from doing what it has always done, which is to have an international presence that allows us to represent our interests."

St-Pierre Plamondon made his comments to reporters on Tuesday, following a meeting he had at his office with Bloc Québécois Leader Yves-Francois Blanchet (pictured on his right) in Quebec City. (Jacques Boissinot/The Canadian Press)
St-Pierre Plamondon added that Quebec will continue to assert its place on the world stage over the coming months.
Not the first public spat for Carney and Quebec premier
Earlier this month, the Quebec premier accused the federal government of attempting to muzzle him, when Carney denied him speaking time at the 21st Canada-EU summit that was held in Montreal.
St-Pierre Plamondon opted to withdraw from the summit and sent Quebec's chief diplomat, Pascal Paradis, to represent him during the summit's activities.
Paradis has also been tasked with being the province's chief negotiator, including taking over the trade file with the United States.

items: Former MNA Pascal Paradis named chief negotiator, diplomat for the PQ

blocks.text: Quebec Liberal Party Leader Charles Milliard said it never would have crossed his mind to boycott the event if he were premier.
"Sulking isn't an option," said the Leader of the Opposition. "I don't think this is the best start to relations between Quebec and Ottawa."
Carney said at the time that it was St-Pierre Plamondon's choice to leave his seat at the table empty.
The prime minister has not yet had an in-person meeting with Quebec's new leader, who was sworn in on Oct. 21.
St-Pierre Plamondon has insisted that their first meeting take place in Quebec City, which the prime minister's schedule has reportedly not been able to accommodate so far.

On Tuesday, however, the prime minister was campaigning in Saint-Hyacinthe-Bagot-Acton ahead of a byelection scheduled there for Dec. 7. The Quebec electoral district is about a two-and-a-half-hour drive from the provincial capital.
Carney and St-Pierre Plamondon are set to meet in meet in Cambodia during the Francophonie Summit later this month.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Patricia Kozicka is a digital journalist with CBC Montreal. She has previously worked in Toronto and Edmonton. You can reach her at patricia.kozicka@cbc.ca.
With files from CBC'S Cathy Senay, Radio-Canada's Jérôme Labbé and The Canadian Press

articles.title: Irving Oil, Grant Enterprises plead guilty to environment charges over N.B. diesel spill next to Tim Hortons
articles.summary: Irving Oil Ltd. and Grant Enterprises 1984 Ltd. have pleaded guilty in provincial court to charges under the Clean Environment Act due to a 200,000-plus-litre diesel spill in Woodstock.

image.caption: Irving Oil and Grant Enterprises pleaded guilty to one charge after more than 200,000 litres of diesel spilled at a Woodstock gas station in late 2024. (Shane Fowler/CBC News)

blocks.text: New Brunswick·New
Irving Oil Ltd. and Grant Enterprises 1984 Ltd. have pleaded guilty in provincial court to charges under the Clean Environment Act due to a 200,000-plus-litre diesel spill in Woodstock.
$400,000 fine recommended as punishment for spilling over 200,000 litres of diesel
Irving Oil Ltd. and Grant Enterprises 1984 Ltd. have pleaded guilty in provincial court to charges under the Clean Environment Act related to a massive diesel spill in Woodstock.
The spill was discovered in December 2024 after a Tim Hortons on Beardsley Road reported its water was contaminated with fuel. The Tim Hortons is next to Murray's Irving gas station and restaurant.
In Woodstock court on Tuesday, it was revealed that the total spill was between 210,000 and 250,000 litres over four months, which is more than previous estimates.

Irving Oil and Grant Enterprises were originally charged with two counts. The charge of failing to immediately report the leak was dropped. The companies pleaded guilty to a charge of releasing a contaminant into the environment.
Crown prosecutor Patrick Wilbur read an agreed statement of facts that said the leak stemmed from a faulty elbow fitting that fed diesel into a 100,000 litre storage tank.
Grant Enterprises had the tank and fill pipe installed in 2014. One of the fittings on that pipe was made of aluminum when it should have been steel or fiberglass.
“Aluminum alloy elbows were never approved nor permitted, and aluminum … should not be part of an underground petroleum system,” Wilbur read.
A faulty aluminum elbow pipe leading to an underground diesel storage tank was found to be responsible for the leak. (Province of New Brunswick)
The cleanup began after inspectors detected the leak along the nearby Trans-Canada Highway.
Wilbur said in court that cleanup recovered about 195,000 litres of diesel. The cleanup and remediation has cost about $15 million so far and the amount will continue to grow.
He also explained how this much diesel being lost into the ground should have been noticed.
“The governance system that includes people, processes and technologies were not being followed.”
Wilbur said regulations for operating the storage tank requires the owner or operator to measure the level of the tank and compare it to how much has been sold.
He said action should be taken immediately if the comparison shows losses.

“While the measurements were taken, the process failed in that it did not detect the ongoing loss that occurred with each delivery,” said Wilbur. “It was not caught by the systems in place for the four months.”

At least 174,000 litres of diesel recovered from gas station leak in Woodstock, province says

blocks.text: There have now been various other systems put in place, including 42 groundwater monitoring wells and 20 drilled wells.
The Crown has requested a total fine of $400,000 with some of the money earmarked for the province’s environmental trust fund. The two companies did not disagree with the amount.
Judge Rose Campbell said she’ll review the case and come back with her sentence on Feb. 8, 2027.

articles.title: Alberta's United Conservative Party faces backlash for pledge that limits riding presidents' independence talk
articles.summary: Some senior party organizers refuse to sign a new NDA stating they'll "abide by" the referendum result.

image.caption: Alberta Premier Danielle Smith has urged the pro-independence members of her United Conservative Party to embrace staying in Canada in the aftermath of October's referendum. (Jeff McIntosh/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Calgary·New
Some senior party organizers refuse to sign a new NDA stating they'll "abide by" the referendum result.
Party organizers refuse to sign NDA demanding they 'abide by' referendum result

The UCP is facing pushback from some of its top organizers for demanding all riding presidents sign a non-disclosure agreement that declares they “recognize, respect and will abide by” results of the separation referendum.

This new demand comes weeks after three-quarters of Albertans voted to keep the province in Canada rather than pursue independence — and Premier Danielle Smith urged UCP members to accept the outcome and move on, or leave for another party.

Party brass recently made candidates for upcoming provincial board elections sign a declaration that they will abide by the referendum decision. Now it’s extending that condition to all 87 current presidents of UCP constituency associations.

“I understand and acknowledge that my public statements and actions as a CA president will have a direct impact on the reputation of the CA and the association,” says the combination NDA and code of conduct sent by party executive director Dustin van Vugt, and obtained by CBC News.
“Accordingly, I wish to clearly state that I recognize, respect, and will abide by the majority decision made by Albertans on Question #10 of the 26/10/19 referendum.”
In an email to riding presidents, van Vugt requested they all sign and return the pledge by this Friday.
But multiple riding presidents are reluctant or unwilling to sign the document, and are calling it an unfair way to stifle their speech.
“It’s not wise to be trying to suppress when we should be trying to unify,” said Darrell Komick, president of the United Conservative association for Calgary-Lougheed.
“That’s the sort of thing that will stop people from volunteering.”

Komick has led one of the party’s most outspoken local groups, having hosted past forums that questioned Alberta’s place within Canada and the safety of COVID vaccines. He also ran unsuccessfully for party president last fall, promising a greater embrace of the pro-independence position.
“As the party of free speech, we should understand that that comes with risks as a party, but it also comes with rewards,” Komick told CBC News.
Darrell Komick, president of the UCP riding association for Calgary-Lougheed, has hosted many forums on contentious topics like vaccine safety. (Youtube/Alberta Politics)

The riding presidents opposed to the party’s new NDA span both sides of the referendum question that has divided party members. One said that at least 15 presidents are signing their own letter to the party explaining that they refuse to endorse the NDA.

“It appears a jam-down by certain people at the upper reaches of the party to squash any public embarrassment or public conflict about independence, and it’s just wrong,” said one president, who did not want to use their name for fear of retribution.
This president, who opposes Alberta independence, questioned why only one divisive issue is highlighted in this non-disclosure form.
“We have back and forth about friggin’ abortion,” said the constituency president. “Why are we singling out this one issue? It’s just ridiculous.”

The source said this agreement appears at odds with a section of the party’s existing code of conduct, which says that constituency association board members shall “not be reprimanded or disciplined by the party... or CA board for exercising their freedom of expression unless such expression constitutes an offence under the Criminal Code of Canada.”
United Conservative officials did not reply to CBC News’ questions before deadline.
Independence supporters at the referendum-night watch party on Oct. 19. Polls suggest that half or more of UCP supporters backed the pro-independence option on the referendum. (Julia Wong/CBC)

Even though Smith had repeatedly declared support for keeping Alberta within Canada, detractors accused her of being too supportive of the separatists within UCP ranks, and making it easier to get the independence question onto the ballot.

But in the days after October’s resounding pro-unity decision, Smith declared the United Conservatives are clearly pro-unity as a party, and that no candidates or MLAs would be allowed to support independence.

“It also means we expect every member of our provincial board and members of constituency association boards across the province to uphold the position of our party on this issue,” the premier said in a video statement to party members last month.
While it was vastly unpopular among most segments of Albertans, about half of UCP supporters supported the pro-independence option in the referendum, according to polling before the vote.
The premier has since faced pockets of resistance from her UCP base, including separatist activists frustrated she took sides in the referendum.

Five riding associations have endorsed subjecting Smith to a leadership review, although most other party constituency groups passed motions opposing a review, meaning that her place in the party is under no immediate threat.

Some pro-independence activists are running for places on the UCP provincial board at the party convention in Calgary later this month. They endorsed the declaration that they’d abide by the unity referendum’s results, but said they’d continue to freely advocate for more “sovereignty” for Alberta within Canada in the short term.
Alberta federalist sees 'a great schism' in separatist movement post referendum
While non-disclosure agreements and codes of conduct are not unusual for not-for-profit organizations, it’s odd to see a policy declaration tucked inside it, one governance expert told CBC News.

“When you're involved in a governing body, you can't pre-commit your political stance,” said Nolan Crouse, instructor and lead expert with the board development program at MacEwan University in Edmonton.

“When I walk into a meeting, I'm supposed to be open-minded. But the verbiage here looks like that the provincial association is pre-committing you to a political stance or [to] ‘abide by’ something, right?”
Crouse, the former mayor of St. Albert, said he’s surprised the form passed “the acid test” among UCP’s leadership and top governance officials.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Jason Markusoff is a CBC producer and writer. He analyzes what's happening — and what isn't happening, but probably should be — in Calgary, in Alberta and sometimes farther afield. He's covered Alberta for more than two decades, previously reporting for Maclean's magazine, Calgary Herald and Edmonton Journal. He appears regularly on Power and Politics, West of Centre and various other CBC current affairs shows. Reach him at jason.markusoff@cbc.ca

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Sara Duterte Impeachment Trial (November 11, 2026)
articles.summary: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will continue on Wednesday, November 11, 2026, with the Defense presenting witnesses to debunk the allegation of unexplained wealth of Duterte.

blocks.text: Published November 11, 2026 6:35am Updated November 11, 2026 6:38am
Sara Duterte impeachment trial Day 42: What to expect
The Defense will present on Wednesday its fourth witness for Article II of the impeachment case, concerning allegations on Vice President Sara Duterte’s unexplained wealth.

Atty. Suzette Balucanag-Punay, the corporate counsel for Gencorp Industries, Inc. and Metro City Chow Foods Corporation — two of the entities linked to the Vice President — will be called to the witness stand this morning, according to defense lead counsel Sheila Sison.

Balucanag-Punay is set to testify on relevant corporate and business matters linked to Duterte and produce certified true copies and/or original copies of the General Information Sheets, Audited Financial Statements, and other related corporate records from 2022 to 2025.

She was supposed to testify on Monday, but was unable to attend the hearing due to a scheduled magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan, according to House lead prosecutor and Batangas 2nd District Representative Gerville Luistro.
Dropped witness
Sison also announced that the defense would no longer present Matina Crossing, Davao City Punong Barangay Cindy Colina in the impeachment trial.
Colina was supposed to be the fifth witness of the defense, and was lined up to testify for today.
During the trial on Tuesday, the defense lawyer asked the court to recall the subpoena issued for Colina, and excused her from attending the proceedings.
“This is of course without prejudice to any subsequent motion that we will make on the court’s taking judicial notice of the geographical divisions with respect to the subject barangay,” Sison said.

Colina was supposed to testify on matters relating to Matina Crossing and to identify and bring all documents related to its creation, official name, and other names upon which it is known whether by official acts, usage, or custom. —Giselle Ombay/BAP/KG, GMA News

articles.title: N.S. group apologizes for including woman convicted in a brutal killing on a panel
articles.summary: The Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia is apologizing after it hosted a panel discussion on violence that featured Marissa Shephard. Shephard was sentenced to 12 years in jail after she…

image.caption: Marissa Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with Baylee Wylie's killing. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Nova Scotia·New

The Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia is apologizing after it hosted a panel discussion on violence that featured Marissa Shephard. Shephard was sentenced to 12 years in jail after she pleaded guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of Baylee Wylie.
Marissa Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with Baylee Wylie's killing
A Nova Scotia group that supports at-risk women and girls is apologizing after it hosted a panel discussion on violence that featured a woman convicted in the brutal killing of a teenager.
Marissa Shephard was listed as a panel member for the event last week organized by the Elizabeth Fry Society of Mainland Nova Scotia.
In 2021, Shephard was sentenced to 12 years in jail after she pleaded guilty to manslaughter and arson in the death of 18-year-old Baylee Wylie, who was stabbed 200 times.
Wylie's body was found in Shephard's burned out townhouse in Moncton, N.B., in December 2015.
Shephard was one of three people sentenced in connection with Wylie's killing.

Devin Morningstar was found guilty of first-degree murder in 2016, while Tyler Noel pleaded guilty in May 2017 to second-degree murder and arson with disregard for human life, and both received life sentences.

items: Parole board imposes strict conditions on Marissa Shephard's release from prison
Marissa Shephard pleads guilty to manslaughter, arson

blocks.text: The Nova Scotia chapter of the Elizabeth Fry Society issued a public statement Monday night saying it made a serious mistake while planning the event.

"Our work asks us to consider everyone who may be affected by violence, and above all, to do no further harm. With this event, our actions did not reflect that, and we have harmed those we support," reads the statement.
The non-profit group said in an email they would not be taking part in media interviews at this time.

"Our staff have received repeated threats of violence, and our priority right now is the safety of our team and the people we support, and respect for families who are grieving," reads the emailed statement sent Tuesday afternoon.

According to court documents, Wylie, Shephard and the two other young men gathered at her home for "some drug-fuelled excitement" that ended tragically with Wylie being tied to a chair, beaten and stabbed repeatedly with a variety of weapons.
