articles.title: Disgraced former leader Sheikh Hasina plans return to Bangladesh after two years in exile
articles.summary:
Hasina fled to India in 2024 after mass uprising. She faces death penalty upon return

Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of…
articles.byline: Hannah Ellis-Petersen and Aakash Hassan in Delhi

blocks.text: Sheikh Hasina is “confident” she will return to Bangladesh in December, according to exiled members of her party, after the disgraced former prime minister of Bangladesh applied for a fresh passport this week.

Hasina has been living in self-imposed exile since August 2024 when she was toppled from power by a mass uprising against her authoritarian rule. She fled over the border to India, where she has since been allowed to live freely in Delhi.

Last November, a tribunal in Bangladesh found Hasina guilty of crimes against humanity and sentenced her to death over her deadly crackdown on a student uprising that left an estimated 1,400 people dead.

Her return to Bangladesh is likely to be disruptive for the country where Hasina’s party, Awami League, is still banned and thousands of its members are in jail. Should she be allowed to return, she is likely to be arrested immediately.

Hasina first raised the prospect of going back to Bangladesh in August. Speaking to the Guardian this week, several exiled Awami League leaders also living in India confirmed that Hasina was serious and “confident” about returning by next month. They confirmed that several other party figures had returned to the country in anticipation.

On Monday, a UK lawyer acting on behalf of Hasina, wrote to the Bangladesh high commission requesting a new passport and national identity card to be issued “in a timely fashion”, in a letter seen by the Guardian.

“The reason our leader Sheikh Hasina has applied for a passport is that she genuinely wants to return,” said a party leader based in the Indian city of Kolkata, who spoke on condition of anonymity because he is not authorised to speak to the media on the party’s behalf.

Hasina has rejected the charges of mass murder and crimes against humanity and claimed the tribunal who convicted her was illegitimate. “She is confident about her return, which is why she has applied for a new passport and a national identity card. If the authorities do not issue her a passport, she will apply for a travel pass to make her return to Bangladesh possible,” said the Awami League leader.

Since Hasina’s conviction, Bangladesh government has put pressure on the Indian authorities to extradite the former prime minister. However, the Indian government – which was very close to Hasina while she was in power – has ignored the demands, straining ties between the two countries.

This week, the Bangladesh government have said that as a “terrorist”, Hasina will only be allowed to return under an “acceptable prisoner exchange” under the India-Bangladesh extradition treaty. The chief prosecutor of the tribunal who sentenced Hasina condemned her announcement to return as a “nothing but a political stunt”.
Despite her conviction and the banning of her party, Hasina still commands significant popularity among the thousands of Awami League cadre still in Bangladesh, many who have been driven underground.

Analysts believe her decision to return, despite the risk of arrest, is driven by an attempt to revive her support base and destabilise the newly-elected government, led by prime minister Tarique Rahman. They were brought to power after in February in Bangladesh’s first democratic election in decades.
Since then, the government has struggled with inflation and recent protests that shut down garment factories, which Awami League hopes to use to its political advantage.

Another Awami League leader said all those in exile intended to follow Hasina back to Bangladesh, despite the threat of arrest and jail. Many of those who were close to Hasina over her 15 years in power have faced severe criminal charges since the fall of her government and have been given lengthy prison sentences in absentia.

“All of us are planning to go back. Some of us have been sentenced in absentia by kangaroo courts, and we know we will be jailed. But we are ready to face the consequences and return to our own people. We will fight this politically,” said the senior leader, who is also based in India.

Some senior party figures have already gone back in recent months, including former MP Mustaque Ahmed Ruhi. Ruhi was immediately arrested by police after returning in September and faces prosecution over an alleged murder committed during the 2024 uprising.
“There are serious threats and dangers, but our cadres and leaders are confident and prepared to return to our people,” the leader said.
During their years in exile, Awami League leaders have continued to meet in Kolkata, where many of them are living, and are routinely summoned to Delhi to meet Hasina.

Speaking over email this week, Hasina told the Associated Press she affirmed her decision to go back. “If death is my destiny, I would rather die on the soil of my own country, among my own people,” she said.

articles.title: Why electrification is the climate game changer we need
articles.summary: From EVs and electric buses on the road, heat pumps warming homes and solar panels powering appliances, the shift to electrifying tech is already in full swing. But what exactly does…

image.caption: Replacing fossil fuels with clean electricity is key to cutting emissionsImage: Barbara Gindl/APA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Electrification isn't just a buzzword, it's a lever that could slash energy bills while reducing the world's dependency on coal, oil and gas. Which also means significantly slashing the heat-trapping CO2 emissions that are linked to flooding and extreme heat around the world.

If fuel-importing countries "speed up the electrification of their economies considerably" they could knock more than $400 billion (€357 billion) off their energy import bills by 2035 compared with 2025 levels.
That is according to a recent analysis by the
which also found that such an acceleration could mean the world needs 18 million fewer barrels of oil per day.
What exactly is electrification?

In a nutshell, electrification means replacing technologies that burn fossil fuels such as oil and gas with electric alternatives. That means switching from diesel cars to electric vehicles (EVs), turning off gas heating and using electricity to power heat pumps.

But the way the electricity running these things is generated is also important. In theory, an EV using power created in a coal-heavy electricity grid could be worse for the climate than a car running on gas.
Electricity derived from renewable energy sources such as solar, wind or hydropower on the other hand produces clean power.
How countries are skipping 200 years of carbon emissions
Where are we right now with global electrification?
The booming EV market is the fastest-growing electrification sector. Globally, one in four cars sold in 2025 was electric and since 2020, international sales have increased by almost 600%.
Nonetheless, electricity only covers about 20% of final energy use in the wider global economy, including that used in businesses, factories and people's homes.
It would need to supply more than half of all power by 2050 if we are to avoid runaway heating and the more intense and extreme weather events connected to a hotter climate.
Are there any limitations to what we can electrify?

Some industries and activities are harder to electrify than others. While it's relatively easy to switch to EVs and decarbonize buildings, some industries such as petrochemicals and steel use fossil fuels as raw materials to make products like plastics, fertilizer, detergent or steel.
In addition, while heat pumps work well for low-temperature needs, they can't replace the temperatures needed in steelmaking or cement production.

Independent research organization the World Resources Institute recommends hydrogen, synthetic fuels or other low-carbon alternatives as more viable options than electrification in cases such as ocean shipping and aviation.
Can aviation become more sustainable?
What are the benefits of electrification?
In addition to cutting down on greenhouse gas emissions resulting in cleaner air and limiting global heating, electrification is also more efficient and cheaper in the long run.

A combustion engine in a car wastes as much as 80% of its fuel's energy, mostly to turn it into heat. Only about 20% is converted to actually move the car. Electric motors, on the other hand, convert about 80% of electrical energy into motion.

As the World Resources Institute points out, running all appliances on electricity will increase electricity consumption. Yet total energy costs are likely to be lower, even if electricity becomes more expensive.
Any challenges to electrification?

As electricity needs grow due to the rapid expansion of AI, data centers and the overall shift to a more electrified world, outpaced grids struggle to keep up. This is increasingly holding back the energy transition, delaying the rollout of additional renewable generation, storage capacity, and electrified demand.
According to the IEA, annual grid investment has to increase about 50% by 2030 from today's $400 billion.

There's also a major mismatch between how long it takes to set up new grid infrastructure (5 to 15 years), compared to renewable energy projects (1 to 5 years), and EV charging infrastructure (1 to 2 years).
Experts say we need smarter grids that support a two-way flow of electricity while remaining secure, stable and able to keep up with higher demand as electrification intensifies.

articles.title: DR Congo sentences 66 soldiers to death for being 'cowards'
articles.summary: The Congolese army's fight against rebel groups has long been hampered by disarray within its ranks.

blocks.text: At least 66 soldiers have been sentenced to death in the Democratic Republic of Congo for cowardice, mutiny and refusing to obey orders, local media report.

The sentences followed a trial of 71 soldiers before a military court in Walikale, in North Kivu province, in eastern DR Congo. Four soldiers were acquitted, while another was sentenced to 10 years in prison.
The army said the trial was intended to improve discipline among troops as they battle armed groups in eastern DR Congo.
The region has endured decades of conflict, with fighting continuing between government forces and the Front for the Refoundation of the Nation (FRN), a rebel coalition that includes the M23 group.
The soldiers were reportedly arrested on 20 October in Walikale, where they were accused of abandoning their positions and fleeing during clashes with FRN fighters.
The Congolese army's campaign against armed groups, including the M23, has long been undermined by poor discipline and disorganisation within its ranks.
The government has repeatedly accused neighbouring Rwanda of supporting the M23, an allegation denied by both Kigali and the rebels despite overwhelming evidence.
The army has faced persistent criticism over its lack of professionalism and disciplined, while soldiers have complained of poor pay and inadequate equipment.
Last month, another 27 soldiers were sentenced to death on similar charges of cowardice after reportedly withdrawing from the frontline during clashes with rebels.
In March 2024, DR Congo lifted a 20-year moratorium on the death penalty, citing the need to remove "traitors" within the army.
The government said capital punishment would also apply to people involved in armed groups, insurrection, as well as committing treason and war crimes.
The decision to reinstate the death penalty was widely criticised by rights groups. However, no formal executions have been carried out since the moratorium was lifted.
Since the beginning of 2025, at least 507 soldiers have been convicted, including 381 death sentences, according to figures compiled by French broadcaster RFI.

In October 2025, former Congolese President Joseph Kabila was sentenced to death in absentia on charges including war crimes and treason. He denied the accusations, but did not appear in court to defend himself. He has since been named as the FRN's leader.

articles.title: Will Australia push for fossil fuel exit at UN talks?
articles.summary: The heat is on Australia as chief negotiator at the COP31 UN climate conference to forge a path away from coal and gas, and to protect Pacific neighbors facing rising sea levels.

image.caption: Australia will lead talks to address the climate crisis, yet remains the world's second-largest exporter of carbon-heavy coalImage: DW

blocks.text: In its role as president of negotiations at the upcoming UN climate talks in Turkey, Australia is being pressured to guide nations towards unified action on slashing the greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions that are generated in large part by burning fossil fuels.
The nation has pledged to lead by example at the summit through a strong commitment to renewable energy, electrification and reduced reliance on planet-heating coal, oil and gas.

"Renewable energy, grids, storage and electrification are creating opportunities to strengthen resilience, improve energy security, and reduce emissions at the same time," said Australian climate minister Chris Bowen in October during a meeting in Fiji ahead of the COP climate conference.
"These are proven, commercial and scalable today. Now is the moment for faster implementation."

Yet Australia is also the world's third-largest exporter of fossil fuels. And unlike France and Germany, or island nations from Fiji to the Bahamas that are highly vulnerable to a changing climate, the COP31 co-president has not yet commited to phasing them out.
As calls grow for the country to set a clear route to a clean energy future, critics say its vague promise to transition away from polluting sources of power does not go far enough.

blocks.caption: Australia is planning for 82% renewable electricity in its grid by 2030. But fossil fuel projects continue to be approvedImage: ACT Government

blocks.text: Transition is also about energy security
Australia is home to 56% of global coal mine projects currently in the pipeline, notes environmental non-profit, 350.org.

Andreas Sieber, head of political strategy at the organization, is calling on the country, the world's second-largest coal exporter, to reverse course and announce an "overdue coal phaseout date" during the COP31 conference.
"Australia needs to walk the walk and follow Germany's example and commit to a phaseout," said Melanie Pill, founder of the Climate Project, an Australia-based climate policy advisory.
The argument to end fossil fuel production is not only about cutting emissions but reducing dependence on energy systems that rely on volatile oil and gas markets, she explained.
"A fossil phaseout in the face of the enduring and escalating conflict in the Middle East is in the interest of everyone," Pill told DW.
How Iran war energy crisis strengthens case for renewables

This is especially true for Australia's diesel-reliant Pacific neighbours, who spend up to 25% of GDP on fossil fuel imports — as opposed 6% on health — according to a report by the Institute for Climate Risk and Response at the University of New South Wales.
As lead negotiator at the UN climate talks, Australia can "flip the narrative" on a fossil fuel phaseout, using the challenge of energy security as a justification, said Pill
Climate tsar still pushing coal and gas
This opportunity could be lost, however, if Australia fails to address fossil fuel exports that accounted for 80% of its total carbon footprint in 2022 — and near 5% of global emissions.

While the nation is a world leader in rooftop solar, and generates around half of its electricity from renewables, this progress is "being undone by its continued approval of more fossil fuels for export," said Simon Bradshaw, COP31 lead and climate expert at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

He notes that the Labor government of Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has approved the construction, expansion or extension of 38 coal, oil and gas projects since coming to power four years ago on a pro-climate platform.

"You cannot aspire to lead on climate abroad if you're not getting your own house in order," said Thomas Houlie, climate and energy policy analyst at Climate Analytics, a global climate policy institute.

Last year, when Australia approved the extension of a major gas export project in the country's west until 2070, Albanese justified the move in the name of a balance between "security of energy supply" and "support [for] the transition which reduces our emissions."

blocks.caption: Australian coal arriving in China contributes to the 5% of global emissions derived from Australian fossil fuel exportsImage: Chen Weifeng/ChinaFotoPress/MaxpppP/picture-alliance

blocks.text: The country has publicly backed a global transition away from the fossil fuels driving the global temperature rise linked to extreme heat and drought. Both through the Global Stocktake agreed at the 2023 UN climate summit, and via the inaugural "transitioning away" summit in Colombia this April, at which Australia and 56 countries pledged to develop a fossil fuel exit roadmap.
But these commitments are not reflected in Australian resources policy, or its domestic rollout of clean power infrastructure.

"While the government has set a renewables target for electricity, it leaves plenty of blind spots in other sectors," said Houlie, adding that emission reductions in industry and transport have been limited and that the push to achieve an 82% renewables target for the electricity grid by 2030 is behind schedule.
Australia needs to step up for Pacific neighbors

In its role as lead negotiator at COP31, Australia has promised to ensure that any final conference text serves to "elevate the views and the experiences" of small Pacific nations in its region from Vanuatu to Tuvalu.

These island countries that generate low emissions yet suffer extreme climate impacts from worsening cyclones or rising seas are "sick of Australia's double talk on climate," said Shiva Gounden, Head of Pacific at Greenpeace Australia Pacific.

Australia must commit to "substantial new funding contributions" to help Pacific neighbors adapt to the climate emergency and achieve energy independence, said Simon Bradshaw. He reiterated the need to concurrently create a "national road map" away from coal and gas production and export.

A Climate Analytics report co-authored by Houlie outlines a fossil fuel phaseout pathway for Australia that can begin immediately. This includes an end to coal power generation by 2034 and a rapid reduction in oil and gas consumption with renewables generating almost all the country's electricity by 2040. Fossil fuel export projects would be eliminated, and existing ones shuttered before becoming obsolete.
"This co-presidency is a golden opportunity for Australia to step up and commit to a phaseout," said Houlie.
Tuvalu – living with the reality of climate change

articles.title: Grenades, grief and a deepening political divide: five takeaways from Sonia Gandhi’s new memoir
articles.summary:
From the assassinations of her husband and mother-in-law to press stonewalling under Modi, Belonging offers an insider’s account of India’s political evolution

Few love stories have been as…

blocks.text: Few love stories have been as closely entwined with a nation’s history as that of Sonia and Rajiv Gandhi. The former’s much-awaited political memoir, Belonging, offers a strikingly candid account of her journey from a small town in Italy to the highest echelons of power in India – all for love, she says.

The veteran Congress party leader has been fiercely protective of her personal world. In Belonging, she opens up for the first time about the extraordinary twists and turns of a life that has largely unfolded in full public view. (The Guardian’s Hannah Ellis-Petersen has a rare in-person interview with Gandhi, and you can read an excerpt from the book here.)

Belonging, published today, contains moving glimpses of Gandhi’s private grief. She writes about the loss of her first child, who died shortly after birth, and the chilling discovery of grenades in a room of their house after Operation Blue Star, the 1984 military operation against Sikh separatists at the Golden Temple in Amritsar. She also provides a ringside view of several turbulent chapters in Indian politics, not least the violent assassinations of her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, in 1984 and her husband, Rajiv, in 1991.

Her book also revisits some of the darker episodes that have dogged the Gandhi family and the Congress party, including Indira’s imposition of the Emergency in June 1975, a 21-month period during which civil liberties were suspended, political opponents were jailed and the press was gagged, which caused fear and dismay across the country. In Gandhi’s account, italso caused a rift within the family.

Ultimately, Gandhi’s memoir is a vivid record of six decades of India’s political transformation from the Congress-dominated secular republic she moved to in 1968 until today, when Hindu nationalism has become the dominant political force under Narendra Modi.
Here are five key takeaways from her memoir and what they reveal about the state of Indian politics today.
Gandhi has had no real contact with Modi for the last 12 years

blocks.caption: Sonia Gandhi, widow of former Indian prime minister Rajiv Gandhi, shown in March 1998 when she was elected president of Congress party. Photograph: John Mcconnico/AP

blocks.text: Gandhi’s account offers a glimpse of how deep the political polarisation runs in Indian politics today. In one revealing passage, Gandhi writes that she has had “practically no real contact” with Modi in the 12 years he has led the nation. In fact, at times when the two have been in the same rooms, such as the speaker’s small chamber, Modi “tends to look away, avoiding eye contact”, she says. On occasion, she adds, he has asked briefly about her health after a hospital stay.

For her, this breakdown is a departure from the past, when leaders on opposing sides of the aisle “would treat one another with cordiality”. After the 2001 terror attack on parliament, Gandhi immediately called then-BJP prime minister AB Vajpayee to enquire about his safety, a gesture he appreciated.

Gandhi sees an increasingly authoritarian style of politics, in which those in power seek to “belittle and torment” opponents. For years, Gandhi’s son, Rahul, has been the subject of BJP’s ridicule, which calls him Pappu, a derisive term intended to portray him as inexperienced and naive. She adds that similar things are happening elsewhere in the world, an observation that can be read in the context of US President Donald Trump’s use of personal insults and ridicule against opponents.
It’s lonely at the top for India’s female politicians

India has an illustrious history of women occupying top leadership positions, long before many other democracies. But their rise has often come at a cost – that of loneliness in navigating a male-dominated political world.

In the book, Gandhi describes a 2012 conversation with Hillary Clinton on the countrys’ female leaders and their backgrounds. In her recollections of Indira, she shares that, despite wielding authority, Indira could feel besieged and profoundly alone, and this was particularly acute, Gandhi writes, in the months leading up to the declaration of the Emergency by her mother-in-law.
Gandhi also writes of her own isolation, including when she decided to take on the leadership of the Congress out of a sense of duty to her family’s political legacy.
Those in power are increasingly stonewalling the press

blocks.caption: A poster showing Indian prime minister Narendra Modi at a protest by the Congress party and its allies in New Delhi on 1 November. Photograph: Manish Swarup/AP

blocks.text: Among the many ways in which Gandhi charts the erosion of India’s democratic conventions in Belonging, one particularly telling shift is the changed relationship between the media and those in power. She recalls a time when journalists had opportunities to question prime ministers directly.

In 12 years in power, Modi has not addressed a single press conference on his own. He has sat in on one press briefing at the conclusion of an election campaign, and appeared alongside US presidents at joint press encounters after bilateral meetings, where they took questions from the press. Modi has consistently avoided facing journalists in an open forum, and his media interactions have largely been one-on-one interviews with sympathetic, pro-government news anchors or in one much publicised exchange with a Bollywood actor who asked him how he liked to eat mangoes.
And it’s not just media …

The book’s publication has brought renewed attention to concerns about the space for free expression in contemporary India, and the extent to which apprehensions about repercussions may influence what can be said, written and published.

Penguin Random House India was to publish Gandhi’s memoir but withdrew from the project in August. Gandhi told the Guardian that it was “uneasy in general with the criticism of the government” and said it had dropped the book after she declined certain suggested edits. Penguin has disputed her account, saying that the suggestion it decided not to publish the book because of refused editorial changes “does not accurately reflect the circumstances”.
The book, released in the US by Alfred A Knopf, is being published in India by HarperCollins.

In June, Penguin had also pulled out of plans to distribute graphic journalist Joe Sacco’s The Once and Future Riot, about the 2013 Muzaffarnagar communal violence. The publisher cited an inaccurate map of India and unresolved citation issues. Sacco, however, blamed the decision on the “current political climate in India”.
She’s had quiet fallouts with the ‘thoroughly dishonest’

Western political memoirs, particularly by former heads of government or senior politicians, are often forthcoming in naming political adversaries, recounting private exchanges and offering candid assessments of colleagues. David Cameron’s 2019 memoir, For the Record, took aim at his former friend, Michael Gove, describing him as “mendacious” and a “foam-flecked Faragist”.
after newsletter promotion

Gandhi, in contrast, is restrained. She writes warmly of the closeness between the Gandhi family and that of Bollywood superstar Amitabh Bachchan, whose parents she lived with when she first moved to India, but she makes no mention of the subsequent estrangement between the two families. In another instance, she does not name the political leader she describes as “thoroughly dishonest” and who she says she trusted in 1999, when Congress unsuccessfully attempted to form a coalition government.
What else we’re reading about

blocks.caption: A painting from the series, When No One Moves by Baaraan Ijlal, who is showing at Art Mumbai. Photograph: Artist Baaraan Ijlal

blocks.text: Art | Art Mumbai runs from 12-15 November at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse. Among the highlights of this year’s edition is artist Baaraan Ijlal’s collaboration with the celebrated lyricist Javed Akhtar, turning his evocative Urdu couplets into paintings. The two will be in conversation with curator Ranjit Hoskote on Friday.

Government | The official bungalow of Andhra Pradesh’s chief minister, N Chandrababu Naidu, was renovated by a government-owned enterprise for Rs 6.5 crore (£518,000), according to the Indian Express (£). The renovation work on the Delhi property included was said to have had a major makeover.

Film | Bollywood’s ambitious rendering of Hindu epic Ramayana, starring Ranbir Kapoor and Sai Pallavi, was released on 5 November. Touted as the most expensive Indian film ever made, it earned praise from the Guardian’s Peter Bradshaw, who described it as “thoroughly engaging, rousing and spectacular”.
Your Diwali celebrations
Readers from India and around the world on the festival of lights and tell us how they celebrated.

blocks.caption: Diwali celebrations have touched readers around the world. Photograph: Firdous Nazir/NurPhoto/Shutterstock

blocks.text: double quotation markIn India, Diwali comes to you. You can see it in the streets, hear it in the neighbourhood and feel it in the atmosphere. In the UK, it is different. Life carries on around you. But traditions do not have to disappear when you move countries – they can change shape. A small light in a quiet room can carry the same meaning as an entire street illuminated for Diwali. Aman, Plymouth, UK

double quotation markMy favorite part of Diwali back home was getting up before sunrise on Narak Chaturdashi and having a ceremonial bath, followed by a breakfast of traditional Marathi Diwali snacks. I have been living abroad for over 10 years now and it’s always a bittersweet time of the year where I miss my family and the general vibe of Diwali in India. But I am trying to build new traditions as one half of an Indian-Austrian couple, which includes trading the traditional boxes of mithai for Manner Schnitten and marzipan. Charu, Germany

double quotation markThere used to be more of a community spirit to Diwali. As kids, we would be tasked with going door to door, exchanging sweets and snacks with neighbours (sometimes to our great displeasure, because it made for awkward conversation with those we had annoyed with our antics). Nowadays, the celebrations are mostly private. Group celebrations are walled off within exclusive clubs, families light their own fireworks almost competitively, and people send each other sweets through a delivery service. Samyuktha, Chennai
Count it
A number worth knowing
The government has approved the sale of a 60.7% stake in IDBI bank to Canadian Fairfax Holdings for Rs 52,878 crore (£4.22bn).
Vibe check

blocks.caption: Now you see it … freestyler Riswan’s football tricks have gone viral on Instagram. Photograph: Supplied

blocks.text: It’s hard to take one’s eyes off Muhammed Riswan when he’s at work. The 23-year-old football freestyler from Areekode in Kerala’s Malappuram district conjures tricks with the ball in a delicately choreographed dance. It glides between his feet, next it is rolling on to his back right before he leaps into the air to catch it with one hand.
Riswan, who’s been freestyling for eight years, is one of the two Indians to win Instagram Rings 2026 award recognising creators. The other is Chanel model Bhavitha Mandava.

Riswan’s big break came with a video filmed at Keralamkundu waterfall, where he pulled off a freestyle move before gracefully arching the ball into the water. The clip has since clocked more than 600m views. Last year, he was invited to watch his sporting idol, Lionel Messi, play in Argentina.

Do you have any thoughts or responses to this week’s newsletter? Is there anything you’d like us to cover in the future? Share your feedback by replying to this, or emailing us at thisisindia@theguardian.com and we may include your response in a future issue.

Ukraine's Zelenskyy in Denmark for talks with Nordic leaders

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has arrived in Denmark, where he is to hold meetings with Nordic leaders on military support, air defense and energy infrastructure security amid Russia's invasion of his country, Danish authorities said.

"I am proud to welcome President Zelenskyy and the Nordic leaders to Denmark. The Ukrainians' fight for a free Ukraine and a free Europe continues," Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen said in a statement.

articles.title: New Knesset speaker could be key to ousting Netanyahu as Israel’s PM
articles.summary:
Opposition politicians get first chance to take control of levers of power, even as they struggle to form government

Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition…
articles.byline: Emma Graham-Harrison Chief Middle East correspondent

blocks.text: Israel’s new Knesset will be sworn in on Tuesday, giving opposition politicians their first chance to take control of some levers of power, even as they struggle to form a new government to unseat Benjamin Netanyahu.
High on the agenda will be replacing the speaker, who wields immense influence by controlling the legislature’s agenda. The role is currently held by Amir Ohana, a close ally of Netanyahu.
Gadi Eisenkot, the former Israeli military chief who got the presidential mandate to try to form a coalition government at the weekend, may take the role himself, Israeli media reported on Monday.

The effort to wrest away control of the Knesset is significant enough that more than 160 top former security officials, including heads of the military, intelligence and police, warned that rightwing activists were planning to disrupt the day with violent attacks.

“Actors who oppose replacing the Knesset speaker intend to go to the Knesset on the day of the swearing-in ceremony and to prevent the MKs and their family members from entering the building,” a forum of retired commanders, the Democracy’s Protective Wall, warned in a letter to serving security chiefs.
“These same actors are encouraging tens of thousands of citizens who support their stance to come and to help them with their mission,” Ma’ariv newspaper quoted the letter saying.
If Eisenkot does not take the speaker role, opposition parties have agreed that someone from his Yashar party will be the nominee.

The opposition parties hold 67 seats in the 120-seat legislature, enough to install a consensus choice for speaker. All have described the current prime minister as a threat to the state and are keen to start moving against him, despite divides blocking the formation of a coalition.

But several of the Jewish-Israeli opposition parties in his “change” bloc have sworn not to sit with the Palestinian-led parties that hold over a quarter of the bloc’s seats, or even join a minority government that has their backing.
Eisenkot has vowed to broker a national emergency government, promising to achieve it with “creative and unconventional political acts”.
In a sign of challenges ahead, he effectively warned that some election promises would have to be broken to unseat Netanyahu.
“No one will be able to fulfil all the [campaign] promises they made, and all of us will need to compromise. That is also leadership, to know when to decide and set priorities,” he said.
There have been protests across Israel urging Jewish-Israeli opposition parties to put unseating Netanyahu ahead of a racist commitment to excluding Palestinian-led parties from government.

Palestinian citizens of Israel make up about 20% of Israel’s population and voted in unprecedented numbers this year, giving them 19 seats. Without them, the opposition bloc has fewer seats than Netanyahu’s diminished coalition.

Rightwing opposition leader Avigdor Lieberman has been trying to seek an alternative path to government through an alliance with ultra-Orthodox parties. They have long been Netanyahu allies but have been frustrated by his failure to deliver on the promise to pass broad military draft exemptions for their community into law. Lieberman has campaigned hard for universal conscription, but appears to prefer compromise on this issue to working with Palestinians.
“Has the End of Times arrived?” leading Haredi (ultra-Orthodox) journalist Arye Erlich wrote in a column for Yedioth Ahronoth newspaper.

“Has Avigdor Lieberman … the biggest persecutor of Haredim Israeli politics has seen in decades, suddenly come to believe that he can compromise on a military draft bill and sit in a coalition government alongside the Haredim?”

Even if Eisenkot does broker a coalition deal, he may delay announcing it until Netanyahu’s speaker has been replaced. Netanyahu is a master of political survival and last-minute deals, fracturing past coalitions by luring defectors into his own alliance.
Ohana could delay signing in a new government for up to a week, and some of the opposition do not want to give Netanyahu that much time to attack the pressure points of any fragile deal.

If Eisenkot cannot form a government, the mandate is passed to other leaders and if they too fail Israel must hold elections again. In the meantime Netanyahu and his far-right allies would stay on as a caretaker government.
Although Netanyahu is calling for his opponents to join him in a unity government, a long period of limbo followed by a new vote offers him a likelier path back to power.
If an alternative government takes power, it will be harder for Netanyahu to destabilise it, said Gideon Rahat, chair in political science at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem.
“Once they establish a government, they might be a minority government, it might be hard for them to do things, but nevertheless, they will be governing and it would be hard to oust them.”

articles.title: Polish unity on show in silent march to honour Krakow shooting victims
articles.summary: Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by Saturday's attack, writes Sarah Rainsford.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
Thousands gathered at Krakow's historic Market Square to honour the victims of Saturday's attack
BySarah Rainsford
Southern and Eastern Europe correspondentReporting fromKrakow
Thousands of people joined a silent march through central Krakow on Monday night, in memory of those killed and injured when a gunman went on a violent rampage at the weekend.
The crowd were led by Poland's president and prime minister, the bitter political rivals putting on a rare show of unity after the country's deadliest attack in modern times.
As they reached the historic Market Square, a bugler played from the tower.
Many people were carrying flowers or candles to leave at the shrines that now dot the cobblestones, one marking each spot where someone died.
Fiercely proud of its reputation for safety, Poland has been profoundly shaken by this attack. It has left people struggling to make some kind of sense of what happened.
The alleged gunman has been named as 24-year-old Michal Oksinski by local media.
Critically injured in a shoot-out with police, he did not regain consciousness and died in hospital early on Monday.
Initially, the interior minister claimed that Oksinski was driven by far-right, extremist views. The national prosecutor's office now says that it's too soon to say he was "inspired" by any ideology.

"The minister wanted to win domestic political points. That's not responsible behaviour," Dr Pawel Musialek of the Jagiellonian University suggests, in a country where politics is highly - and often viciously - polarised.
"So far we've seen no clear message that this guy was strongly ideological, and that it's not more like something from the darknet."

There's been no mention of any letter or manifesto that Oksinski left. One neighbour told Polish news site Onet that the 24-year-old was a "bit of a loner" but few who knew him well have spoken publicly.
In addition to his electronic devices like his phone, investigators are examining a number of badges that Oksinski had attached to his military-style outfit.

The prosecutor's office says a yellow Gadsden flag with a coiled snake symbol was displayed in his bedroom. "It has various meanings of freedom and rebellion," a spokesman emphasised. "Not necessarily negative."
It was at Oksinski's home that the bodies of his parents and sister were discovered.
It's alleged that he shot them, before driving some 200km (125 miles) south to continue the killing in Krakow.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Candles and flowers have been placed around the square in places where someone died
Two days on, shops and cafes around the market square are beginning to fill up again, but the mood is subdued.
A Zara clothes shop is still boarded up, after bullets smashed the glass. A local man in his 50s died just outside.
Jo, a Scottish tourist, saw paramedics "who got there ridiculously fast", fighting to save him. "It was all pretty grim."
Like many, she initially mistook the rifle shots for fireworks.
On the opposite corner of the square, beside another cluster of flowers, people keep pausing to take pictures of the holes that were blasted into the wall by gunfire.
One of the six victims has been identified as a Polish painter in her 50s, who was a mother of four, and in town with friends for an exhibition opening.
A British citizen and an Austrian who died are yet to be named publicly.
Several drivers of the horse-drawn carriages that are usually poised to trot tourists around the square were seriously injured.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion

blocks.text: "This is supposed to be a safe place!" Olha, a Ukrainian citizen, moved to Krakow for safety when Russia launched its full-scale invasion
Olha, who works in a nearby chocolate shop says everyone is now nervous.
On Saturday, people rushed into her store to escape the gunman who was tearing around in his car, firing through the window.
Olha is Ukrainian, and moved to Krakow when Russia invaded. "We left our own country for safety. This is supposed to be a safe place!" she exclaimed.
"It's so sad, and so scary. Especially that he drove all the way here for two hours, planning this and thinking about it."
She regrets that the gunman did not survive: "So many are dead, so many lives have been ruined, and now there will be no justice."

blocks.caption: Image caption, Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday

blocks.text: Image source, Filip Radwanski/Anadolu via Getty Images
Political differences were set aside between President Karol Nawrocki (left) and Prime Minister Donald Tusk (right) at the vigil on Monday
When Oksinski's car was searched, four firearms and "hundreds of rounds of ammunition" were found, all owned legally by the alleged killer and his father.
Both were members of the Swit Starachowice sports club, where there is a shooting range. A spokesman recalls Michal Oksinski as unremarkable: average competition results and normal behaviour.
He had been just three times this year, most recently in August with his father. The club spokesman is adamant that it does not train combat firing, only shooting from a fixed point.
Gun ownership in Poland has grown considerably since war broke out in Ukraine just across the border, but this is the first mass shooting anyone here can remember.
Inevitably, it has brought scrutiny of the checks over who qualifies to handle such weapons, including psychological tests, as Michal Oksinski passed all of them.
On Monday, the government announced an urgent review.

blocks.caption: Image caption, "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"

blocks.text: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon"
At the spot where Oksinski's car was intercepted and he was shot by police there is another memorial, this one in honour of the officers still in hospital.
Some have brought flowers, but a girl called Bianka has left a card that reads: "Thank you Mr Policemen, get better soon."
A couple of steps away, there's a series of bullet holes in the glass.
"This man was a real hero, he didn't hesitate," Ania says, referring to officer Jakub Kulik who was shot in the chest. His condition remains serious. "We're here to help him fight for his life."
"Nothing like this has never happened before, it's terrible," a young man called Wojtek tells me.
He's only glad that the gunman responsible for such horror turned out to be Polish.
"People here are already against immigration, so that would have been even worse."
Ania thinks Poles will pull through, though the country's image as a low-crime oasis has been shattered.
Most of all, she's angry that Michal Oksinski died without accounting for the devastation he allegedly wrought.
"I think we deserve to know why."

articles.title: 'Cruise for life' ship seized in Singapore
articles.summary: The ship was meant to take guests around the world, but the trip was cut short after its operator ran out of money.

blocks.text: A round-the-world cruise that left passengers stranded in Cambodia after its US-based operator ran out of money has been seized in Singapore.
The Odyssey, which set off from Belfast in October 2024 and was meant to take guests on a years-long voyage around the world, is now anchored in Singapore port waters, local authorities say.

Around 200 guests were forced to leave the ship last month in the Cambodian port city of Sihanoukville, after its owner Villa Vie Residences abruptly suspended operations citing "extraordinary increases in fuel costs".
The crew onboard are reported to be well, Singapore's port authority said.
"Arrangements for their welfare and wellbeing are being managed by the vessel's creditors," the authority said, adding that the vessel had been "placed under arrest pursuant to a court order".
Singapore law firm Helmsman LLC has been named the "arresting solicitor", but it is not clear which party it represents.
The Odyssey was meant to go on a three-and-a-half-years voyage covering 150 countries.

Passengers were given the options of buying their cabin outright, which allows them to stay onboard beyond its initial voyage, paying for a five-year residency, or renting a cabin for days-long tours.
Permanent residencies in its cabins ranged from $120,000 (£89,272) to $440,000. Those cabins were also available for rent from $3,500 a month, according to its website.
"For roughly the price of a car, you can own your home on a ship that travels the world," its founder Mikael Petterson had earlier said.
However the cruise was beset with problems from the start, with its departure delayed for four months because of repairs and paperwork.

While in Vietnam, crew members reportedly bought food from local grocery stores because the company owed money to a vendor who refused to deliver food, according to CBS News, the BBC's partner in the US.

CBS also reported that the operator warned passengers of its financial troubles in August, when it had sailed on a separate occasion into Singapore, and had to raise money from guests to keep the cruise going.
It had also mentioned the risk of being detained then.
Holly Hennessey, one of the ship's passengers, had earlier told the BBC guests were asked to consider paying a fuel surcharge as prices soared, and that their itinerary had been "severely curtailed".
The vessel sailed again into Singapore earlier this month, weeks after the cruise came to a sudden end while in Cambodia.

As the Iran war sent fuel prices soaring earlier this year, monthly fuel cost per cabin in parts of Asia had risen to as much as $8,000 from $1,800, Villa Vie Residences said in a statement on 27 October.
It added that it had taken "significant steps to reduce fuel consumption" but those measures turned out to be insufficient to offset the "extraordinary increase in fuel costs".
The company also said it was working with residents to "identify temporary living arrangements" while in Cambodia.

articles.title: LIVE UPDATES: Impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte
articles.summary: Bookmark this page for Rappler's comprehensive coverage of Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial at the Senate

blocks.text: The impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte — the first Philippine public official to be impeached twice by the House of Representatives — began at 2 pm on Monday, July 6.

There are four articles of impeachment against Duterte involving alleged misuse of confidential funds, unexplained wealth, bribery of Department of Education officials, and grave threats against President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. and his family.

Only 21 out of 24 senator-judges are physically present. Senator Bato dela Rosa remains in hiding as he faces an International Criminal Court arrest warrant over Rodrigo Duterte’s drug war, Senator Jinggoy Estrada has been detained and suspended in connection with a plunder case, and Senator Rodante Marcoleta surrendered to authorities as he also faces a plunder case.
On this page, we bring you the latest updates, analyses, videos, and photos as the trial of the Vice President unfolds.

articles.title: Epstein associate who still runs model agency 'put me in danger' says abuse survivor
articles.summary: A woman says an agency boss sent her to photoshoots at the sex offender's Florida beach home.
articles.byline: Oana Marocico, Sheida Kiran, Haya Al Badarneh

blocks.text: A woman raped by Jeffrey Epstein says the president of the model agency representing her put her in danger, when he sent her to two photoshoots at the convicted sex offender's Florida beach house.
At the time, in 2009, Epstein was serving a jail sentence for sex offences against a minor but was allowed to work each day from his home.
"My agency's job was to protect me, and they failed. In fact, they put me in danger. And for that, they should be held accountable," she tells the BBC World Service.

Roza was 18 when she was first sent to Epstein's Palm Beach home by MC2 Model Management's US branch, having only arrived in the US from Uzbekistan about a month earlier. MC2's US president at the time, Jeff Fuller, now runs another US model agency called The Source Models.
"My agency knew exactly where I was. So Jeff knew exactly where I was going," says Roza.

She shows us an expense statement suggesting Fuller himself booked her flight home from Palm Beach, following her second shoot at Epstein's home. Fuller has previously claimed he did not know Roza was going to Epstein's house.

She says the photoshoots led to her being employed as an assistant to Epstein. Other survivors have explained how the financier used the recruitment of assistants as an elaborate ruse to allow him to continue abusing young women.
Roza says Epstein went on to systematically rape her.
Fuller has not responded to the BBC's allegations. He has previously said he did not know Roza was being abused.
We discovered through the Epstein-related documents released by the US Department of Justice [DOJ] that 10 models from MC2 met, or were in communication with, Epstein after his conviction.
The files also show Epstein gave $1m (£742,000) to MC2 in 2005 - despite the agency owners telling a US publication two years later that Epstein had no involvement in their company.

Testimony shared with BBC Eye also raises questions about the role played by two other individuals who were active in the model industry, and whom the DOJ files show had close relationships with Epstein - former agent Ramsey Elkholy and agency director Faith Kates.

A DOJ statement from last year, that no evidence has been uncovered which would warrant further investigation against "uncharged third parties", is now being challenged by New York State senator, Zellnor Myrie.
He has proposed a new sex trafficking bill to give police greater power to investigate Epstein's alleged enablers.
If you are outside the UK, please watch on YouTube, external
An email in the DOJ files, from Fuller to Epstein, makes clear the close ties between the agency and the financier.
"Had it not been for you, we would have fired her months ago," Fuller writes of another model in March 2012. "And I would be careful as she blabs about things," he says.

A month after Epstein's second arrest in 2019, MC2's US branch was dissolved and Fuller opened a new agency, The Source Models, which is still operating. The BBC has found that 50 models from MC2 were transferred to his new agency.
We asked The Source Models to comment on our findings - it did not reply.
Model agencies were useful to Epstein, says Sigrid McCawley, the lead lawyer for more than 100 of Epstein's victims.

"Epstein said to many people he wanted three different girls a day. Think about those numbers... The [model] scouts were really critical because they were the ones who were identifying the type of woman that Epstein liked."
In the case of former agent Ramsey Elkholy, BBC Eye has discovered he tried to connect 34 women to Epstein, including an 18-year-old who was still in school.
The experience of one of the women highlights how assistants would be co-opted into the structure of the abuse.
Elkholy, the DOJ files show, suggested to Epstein that one of the financier's female assistants befriend this woman, before introducing her to Epstein.
We spoke to this woman, and she revealed that at her first meeting with Epstein, aged 19, he sexually abused her in his New York townhouse.

Ramsey Elkholy told the BBC: "I completely reject any allegation that I knew of or facilitated abuse of any kind… At the time, I had no knowledge of any abuse and I knew only his own [Epstein's] account of his 2008 [legal] case, which I misguidedly believed."

He continued: "The record and published reporting show that women were often groomed by other women in his inner circle. I was never part of that circle, or indeed of any such activity… my intention was to help models find professional opportunities by introducing them to an extremely well-connected individual."

items: If you are in the UK and you have been affected by any of the issues in this story such as sexual abuse and violence, information and support is available at BBC Action Line

blocks.text: Lawyer Sigrid McCawley says these female assistants would have had "no choice" in how they conducted themselves.
"These young survivors were being abused regularly. Their livelihoods were being threatened… They had to do what they were being told to do."
Another model we have spoken to, Simona (not her real name), from eastern Europe, told us Epstein had raped her more than 200 times.
"People think that we gained something, that we agreed on this abuse in order to gain something, whether it's monetary or influential, but it's not true. We're left with deep trauma," says Simona.
She says the first time she met the financier, aged 20, she was already signed with a model agency in New York, and he offered to introduce her to his "good" friend Faith Kates.

At the time, Kates was the head of Next Management, one of the world's biggest model agencies. She stepped down from that senior executive position in December last year, but is still legally listed as a director of the company.
Simona says at this meeting, Kates suggested she undergo plastic surgery and sent details of a surgeon to Epstein.
After her meeting with Kates, Simona says Epstein convinced her to stop modelling.
And just like Roza, and several other of his victims, she became his assistant. She says he went on to rape her and control every aspect of her life for nearly two years.
The DOJ files show Epstein asked Kates to meet an additional five models, though it is not clear how many of these meetings took place.

Lawyers for Faith Kates told the BBC: "Jeffrey Epstein was a master manipulator... Ms Kates was one of those grossly misled by Epstein. Had she known then what she - and everyone else - now knows, she would have never associated with him."
They added she had never asked a model to have plastic surgery.
We approached Next Management for comment, but it did not reply.

Myrie told the BBC that if his bill were to become law, and "you were sending models to Epstein and you knew what Epstein was doing, or you should have known what he was doing, you will be held accountable".
Roza hopes sharing her story will encourage others to come forward.
"There are many, many survivors out there who never speak, because it's scary. So to all my sister survivors… you know me now. You know my name. I say, reach out."
Additional reporting by Annika Grosser

articles.title: Ukraine peace talks resume with 'some flexibility' by warring sides, US officials say
articles.summary: Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are all sending delegation to the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.

blocks.text: Moscow and Kyiv are privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would controls Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario, US officials have said.
The comments came on the eve of the first trilateral talks aimed at ending the war in Ukraine since February.
Senior officials from Moscow, Kyiv and Washington will meet in Abu Dhabi as the fifth anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine approaches.

Jared Kushner - Donald Trump's son-in-law and part of the US delegation alongside peace envoy Steve Witkoff - said the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.
"An important part of this process is encouraging all parties to begin thinking seriously about what comes after the war," Kushner wrote on X.
But Moscow and Kyiv's positions on ending the conflict in the first place remain far apart.
A key area of disagreement between the two involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is by now mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk which it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those sections, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".
However, he acknowledged that the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it's attacked again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.

Since then, European leaders - who have been largely excluded from peace talks – have pushed to be involved in the process amid concerns that decisions about the security of their continent would be made without them.

European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen urged on Monday to include Nato allies and EU members into any "meaningful discussions about Europe's security architecture". President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly stated Kyiv wanted Europe to be part of the talks.

The US official said the Americans would propose moving into a multilateral format bringing the Europeans into the discussion. "Hopefully we'll get the Russians on board," the official said, while acknowledging that "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans."

Since the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.
Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.
After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine which "might involve all of Europe".
Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result into a fair peace.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believes Trump wants "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.
The only way to make Putin start real negotiations is by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.

"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".
Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi will include Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.

Kyiv is sending several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.

Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.
On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations."
"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."

articles.title: The superpower battle over energy – and what it means for your bills
articles.summary: A tug-of-war between China and the US could have a big impact on energy costs, but who will win?

blocks.text: A gas rig in the North Sea. An oil field in Texas. A solar panel factory in China. They can feel a world away, but your energy bill says otherwise.
In January, it could jump by more than a quarter – around £460 extra a year for the typical UK household – according to the latest forecasts from the big suppliers British Gas, EDF and E.ON.
For the second time in four years, a war thousands of miles away is landing in British inboxes.
Since US and Israeli strikes on Iran in February effectively closed the Strait of Hormuz, oil and gas prices have soared.
Winter is expected to push them higher still: demand for gas is rising just as Europe's winter gas stores are at their lowest since records began in 2011.

And there's a bigger threat looming over all of this: the warming climate. Cutting carbon emissions is essential to limit future warming and avoid the most damaging effects of climate change. But keeping bills down while cutting emissions is proving hard – and not just for the UK.

As world leaders gather this week in Antalya, Turkey, for COP31, the UN climate summit, the same tension is playing out around the world. Energy and climate policy has become the front line in a contest between the world's two energy superpowers, leaving everyone else squeezed in between.

America is betting on fossil-fuel molecules: pumping record volumes of oil and gas and pressing its allies to buy them. China is betting on electrons: flooding the world with the solar panels, batteries and electric cars that can replace those fuels.
Whether the bet on fossil fuels or renewables wins will shape not just what the world pays for energy, but how fast it can cut the emissions that are heating the planet.

The UK, which already buys nearly a quarter of its imported gas from America and much of its clean energy kit from China, is being pulled both ways. So which path will it take? Is there a middle way and what will it all mean for your bills?
Two decisions

On the Moray Firth near Inverness, a long spit of sand and dunes curls out into the sea at Whiteness Head. Behind it lies a yard where, for nearly 30 years, thousands of workers built the giant platforms that opened up North Sea oil.

Ming Yang, one of China's biggest wind turbine makers, wanted to bring it back to life with a £1.5bn factory and up to 1,500 jobs initially generated. In March, after US lawmakers had urged the UK to block it, ministers did just that, citing national security.
Panorama, Fire and Floods: Our Extreme Weather
9 November 2026
Last month, they approved a new North Sea gas field, Jackdaw. No to Chinese wind turbines; yes to North Sea gas.

Few countries are more exposed to the energy shock than the UK. Gas heats most homes and, much of the time, sets the wholesale price of electricity. The last shock, after Russia's invasion of Ukraine, cost households an extra £63bn – around £2,200 each – according to the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit and E3G, two climate and energy research organisations.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Wind turbines represent homegrown energy, but they come with potential problems
Less than half of the UK's gas now comes from its own North Sea fields, and the energy we import often comes from places that turn out to be unstable or unreliable.

At the same time, Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh says tackling climate change remains a priority after Britain's hottest summer on record. The heatwaves, droughts and wildfires it brought would have been almost impossible without global warming, the Met Office's chief scientist told BBC Panorama.
But when I pressed Fahnbulleh on which matters most, bills or climate, she was unequivocal: "With the cost of living biting, affordability is my overriding objective, without a doubt."
"We are far too exposed to global markets we have no control over," Fahnbulleh told me. "What's the solution to that? Homegrown clean energy."
There are two ways to make Britain's energy more homegrown: drill for more of it, or build more of it.
The case for drilling

Within hours of Jackdaw's approval, US President Donald Trump - at war with wind turbines since objecting to a wind farm near his Aberdeenshire golf course in 2006 - took to Truth Social. "They should go FULL BLAST!!!" he wrote. "TAKE DOWN THE COSTLY AND RIDICULOUS WINDMILLS!"
Now the UK government faces a tougher choice - whether to approve Rosebank, west of Shetland, the UK's largest undeveloped oil field.

Rosebank is far bigger than Jackdaw - Fahnbulleh has said it would produce about seven times the emissions - and it is mostly oil, not gas. The subject has reportedly split the cabinet. A decision is expected within weeks.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

blocks.text: Image source, Press Association
Fahnbulleh, centre, at Jackdaw last month. She says the drilling will have minimal impact on energy prices

The government's opponents are already blaming high bills on its reluctance to drill. Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch has told the prime minister to "stop faffing about" and give permission, calling drilling "the only way we can protect families from rising bills".
"If we use our own gas… that will bring our bills down," says Reform UK's Richard Tice.
Last week's US midterms were a reminder of the political risks. Soaring petrol prices are widely seen as a key reason Trump's Republicans lost control of Congress.
But when I asked Fahnbulleh whether producing more British oil and gas would bring bills down, she was clear. "No, it doesn't," she said. "In the end, the oil and gas is sold on global markets."

Critics go further. Rosebank "doesn't really do anything for energy security", argues Tessa Khan of the campaign group Uplift, which has fought the field in the courts. "What it does do is send a very dangerous signal about the UK's seriousness about addressing climate change after the summer that we've just had."

Zoom out, though, and the row looks rather different. The North Sea is in long-term decline. Output has fallen by more than two-thirds since its peak in 1999, and the Office for Budget Responsibility expects it to keep falling by around 10% a year – even with Rosebank, which its forecast assumes goes ahead.

Whatever ministers decide, the basin's most productive days are behind it. Jackdaw's reserves amount to only a few months of UK gas demand, while Rosebank contains less than a year's worth of our oil consumption.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
The debate around Rosebank and Jackdaw has sparked vehement opposition from climate protesters

And last week the government introduced a bill to write its ban on new exploration licences into law. Rosebank, which is already licensed, is not covered. That could let ministers have it both ways: approve the last big field, while promising there will never be another.
With bills set to rise again in January, that may prove a tempting combination.
The case for electrons
The alternative is to build.
Gas is bought, burned and bought again. A wind turbine or solar panel costs money to put up but can then generate electricity for decades without needing shipments of fuel.

The government's climate advisers, the Climate Change Committee, calculate that a future price shock like 2022's would push household energy bills up 59% if Britain stayed on a high-carbon path - but only 4% if it focused on renewables.

The cost of power from new solar farms fell by 90% between 2010 and 2024, and from onshore wind by 70%, according to the International Renewable Energy Agency. But the recent bout of global inflation has been pushing initial costs back up. Last year the Danish developer Ørsted scrapped plans for Hornsea 4, a giant wind farm off the Yorkshire coast, blaming soaring supply chain costs.
Higher interest rates have made things worse. Most of the cost of a wind or solar farm comes up front, so developers must borrow heavily before they generate any power.

And there is another problem. Britain needs expensive new electricity networks to bring that renewable power to the towns and cities where it is needed. Meanwhile, gas-fired stations still frequently set wholesale power prices - meaning any cost savings are not always reflected in customer bills.
All of which means building more renewables does not automatically mean lower household bills.
The China question
And there is another issue - China's dominance of clean tech. It makes the vast majority of the world's solar panels and batteries, and around two-thirds of its electric cars.
And China's lead is growing. In March, its exports of solar panels, batteries and electric cars hit a record, up 70% on a year earlier, according to the think tank Ember.

The UK wants to escape the fossil fuels that leave households exposed to price shocks and keep adding to global warming. Much of the technology needed to replace those fuels comes from China - a country it is increasingly reluctant to depend on.
I asked Fahnbulleh whether Britain was swapping dependence on petrostates for dependence on Beijing. "Well, look, we are," she said, adding: "we've got a diversified global market".
Britain will keep buying from China where it needs to, says Fahnbulleh, but she wants more of the kit made here. "I want to see turbines," she said.
Yet UK-built turbines were exactly what Ming Yang was offering.
"There was a security risk, and national security comes first and foremost," says Fahnbulleh. The government has never publicly explained what that risk was.
Two days before Jackdaw was approved, Japan's Sumitomo Electric opened Britain's first HVDC subsea cable factory at Nigg, a short way up the coast from Whiteness Head, creating up to 250 jobs.
Foreign investment, then - just not from China.
Role reversal

Earlier this year the US formally left the Paris climate agreement and is not expected to send a delegation to this year's COP. Without American pressure, others have less reason to make bold promises: national pledges now add up to a cut in global emissions of just 6% by 2035, the UN says – a tenth of what scientists say is needed to limit warming to 1.5C.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

blocks.text: Donald Trump is a big exponent of fossil fuels

China is beginning to fill the space. Li Shuo, of the Asia Society Policy Institute, calls it a "role reversal". Once "a very conservative player" at climate talks, China now sees pushing the global climate agenda as serving its national interest – and, he says, "we're only at the beginning of this". It aims to hit one of COP31's flagship goals, getting 35% of its energy from electricity, five years early.
And increasingly it is Chinese companies, rather than governments' promises, that are driving the transition. "It's really just a China story," says Li Shuo.
If that is right, it leaves the UK in an uncomfortable place. Hard choices – and they come when household budgets are already stretched thin.

articles.title: Trump says Nvidia boss told him he had no idea woman he had affair with was Chinese spy
articles.summary: The US president said the FBI is now investigating the affair. He said he spoke with Jensen Huang and asked him about the affair.

blocks.text: Donald Trump has said the boss of Nvidia, whose affair with an alleged Chinese spy is being investigated, told him that he had "no idea she was a spy".
The US President said he spoke with CEO Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.
"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair. China has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia, who commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.
Trump said the FBI was also investigating the affair but did not elaborate on the probe or when it was launched.
US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.
